Mortgage refinancing: compare payment relief with the cost of switching

Five graphics compare monthly payments, cash-paid fees, interest, remaining debt and the timing of cost recovery over a common window.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 3 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Compare refinancing over the same remaining-amortization window

Interactive planning lab

Monthly payment reduction / increase$327.13
Payment relief less upfront fees over the window$1,776.79
Interest-cost saving less upfront fees$7,268.92

Hypothetical refinance with the same starting principal and remaining amortization, compared over the selected 1–60 months. Both quoted nominal annual rates are compounded semi-annually and converted to monthly rates, then held fixed for the comparison window only. Payments occur monthly and are calculated separately for each rate; intermediate amounts are unrounded and final payments capped at debt owed. Break charge and other costs are external quote assumptions, paid in cash at time zero and never financed. With zero opening debt there is no modeled refinance or fee. No extra borrowing, amortization extension, blend-and-extend, future renewal, discounting, tax deduction, investment of payment relief, borrower qualification or actual lender penalty formula is calculated. A positive cost advantage means lower modeled interest plus fees over this window, not approval or a complete lifetime recommendation.

The central idea

Compare the same principal, amortization and time window. A payment reduction includes principal-repayment differences, so it is not automatically the financing-cost saving.

01

Get the switching costs before comparing the new rate

The FCAC’s guide to breaking a mortgage contract explains why a lower offered rate must be considered alongside fees and any prepayment charge. It also points out that qualification and other options can affect the decision.

The break-charge control is an external quote assumption. This tool does not estimate an interest-rate differential, select a lender or decide whether the borrower qualifies. Confirm the charge, other closing costs, quote expiry and applicable conditions directly.

All upfront costs are paid from cash in this comparison. They are not added to the new loan, and no additional borrowing is taken. If the actual proposal finances costs or changes the remaining amortization, it needs a different cash and debt schedule.

02

Put both mortgages on the same comparison basis

The default balance is CAD 400,000 with twenty years remaining. The current hypothetical quoted rate is 6%; the proposed rate is 4.5%. Both use nominal annual rates compounded semi-annually and converted to monthly rates for this illustration.

Both loans retain the same remaining amortization, but each has its own calculated monthly payment. The current payment is approximately CAD 2,848.75 and the proposed payment CAD 2,521.62, a reduction of about CAD 327.13.

The comparison lasts thirty-six months, with both rates held constant only within that window. It does not forecast the next renewal. Choose a window for which the rate assumptions are meaningful; a twenty-year amortization does not mean a twenty-year rate commitment.

03

Separate principal repayment from the cost of borrowing

The example enters CAD 8,000 of break charge and CAD 2,000 of other closing costs, totaling CAD 10,000 paid at time zero. That initial cash must be available even though future payments are lower.

Over thirty-six months, modeled interest is about CAD 68,241 on the current loan and CAD 50,972 on the proposed loan. The model’s unrounded interest difference is about CAD 17,269. After upfront costs, the financing-cost advantage is approximately CAD 7,269.

The cost bars exclude principal repayment because it reduces a liability rather than representing interest or a fee. Intermediate amounts remain unrounded until display, so adding independently rounded figures can differ by cents. These are scenario calculations, not a lender’s repayment statement.

04

Check remaining principal alongside the cash released

Cumulative payment relief after the CAD 10,000 upfront cost is only about CAD 1,777 by month thirty-six. The proposed loan also has a lower remaining balance: approximately CAD 360,193 versus CAD 365,685.

The current-minus-proposed debt difference is about CAD 5,492. Adding that liability reduction to cash payment relief gives the approximately CAD 7,269 financing-cost advantage. The two measures reconcile because both choices started with the same debt.

This identity helps explain why payment reduction alone is incomplete. Part of a payment is principal, and the two repayment paths do not retire identical principal amounts during the window. The debt bars are liabilities at the comparison date, not additional charges to add again to the interest-cost bars.

05

Use the two recovery curves and then stress the assumptions

The cash-relief curve and interest-saving curve both begin at negative CAD 10,000. Under the default assumptions, cumulative interest saving covers the cost in month twenty-one, while cumulative payment relief covers it in month thirty-one.

Those crossings answer different questions. The first is an undiscounted financing-cost comparison; the second asks when payment reductions have replenished the cash paid upfront. Neither assumes the released cash earns a return or that later rates remain unchanged beyond the window.

The matrix changes the proposed rate and total cash-paid costs while holding the other terms selected. A positive result means lower modeled interest plus fees in this window. Review liquidity, loan terms, qualification and the possibility of moving or refinancing again before relying on that result. A favorable arithmetic comparison is one part of the decision.
